title: Washington Halts the Advance: Diplomacy Overrides the Battlefield
sources: Balkan Battlegrounds Vol. I, pp. 417-418 (Operation Maestral: Šipovo and Bosanski Petrovac; Jajce restored to Croat hands 13 September 1995)
Balkan Battlegrounds Vol. I, p. 419 (fall of Ključ, 17 September 1995)
Balkan Battlegrounds Vol. I, p. 427 (Operation Južni Potez opens 8 October 1995 under Gotovina, 11-12,000 troops; Mrkonjić Grad falls; Zagreb's Banja Luka calculus)
Balkan Battlegrounds Vol. I, p. 428 (fall of Sanski Most 10 October 1995; HVO stop line 25 km from Banja Luka on 11 October; Dudaković continues past the ceasefire to 20 October)

Balkan Battlegrounds Vol. I, p. 429 (Croatia sidelines itself after Maestral to brake Bosnian gains; Tuđman under US pressure over Banja Luka; Zagreb proceeds with Južni Potez; Izetbegović bows but sets conditions to buy the ARBiH time)

Balkan Battlegrounds Vol. I, p. 462 nn. 821, 823 (Delić urges continued fighting; ARBiH commanders' post-war claims assessed as unlikely; US pressure came in September after Maestral, yet Zagreb ordered Južni Potez in October)
source_note: Editorial provenance: originally machine-drafted, then hand-corrected against Balkan Battlegrounds Vol. I. The correction reverses the compliance direction (Zagreb proceeded with Južni Potez despite US pressure; Sarajevo complied reluctantly while stalling), qualifies the claim that Banja Luka was there for the taking, and replaces the mid-October freeze with the 12 October ceasefire and the fighting that continued to 20 October. The post-Dayton return of Mrkonjić Grad and Šipovo to Republika Srpska is not narrated by Balkan Battlegrounds and is deliberately omitted rather than sourced elsewhere.
content:
By mid-October 1995, Federation forces had achieved what three years of international diplomacy had failed to produce: a territorial division of Bosnia approximating the 51-49 percent split between the Federation and Republika Srpska that had been the basis of every serious peace proposal since the Contact Group plan of July 1994. The combined Croatian-Bosniak ground offensive, launched in the wake of NATO's Operation Deliberate Force, had driven the VRS from approximately a third of the territory it had held since 1992. Sanski Most, Ključ, Jajce, Šipovo, Mrkonjić Grad, and Bosanski Petrovac had all fallen. The road to Banja Luka — the largest city in Republika Srpska and the de facto Bosnian Serb capital — lay open.

Then Washington intervened. US envoy Richard Holbrooke, who had been conducting intensive shuttle diplomacy to bring all parties to the negotiating table, communicated directly with the Croatian and Bosnian governments to halt the advance. The message was blunt: the capture of Banja Luka would produce a humanitarian catastrophe involving hundreds of thousands of Serb refugees, would destabilize the entire region, and would destroy the conditions necessary for a negotiated peace. Neither government simply obeyed. Croatia had already retired to the military sidelines after Operation Maestral in September — less in deference to Washington than to brake the Bosnian government's gains, lest its own partner emerge from the war weighing too heavily in the regional balance. Tuđman was under American pressure not to take Banja Luka, and he did not take it; but he ordered one more operation regardless. Južni Potez opened on 8 October under General Ante Gotovina with eleven to twelve thousand troops, and Mrkonjić Grad fell on the 10th — a reminder to the Serbs that the city could still be lost if they refused to deal. Sarajevo bowed to the American demand and then declined to hurry: Izetbegović set additional conditions for the Serbs to argue over, so that the ARBiH would have more time to gain ground.

The decision was one of the most consequential diplomatic interventions of the entire war. Federation forces were advancing against a disintegrating VRS defense. The Bosnian Serb army, battered by NATO air strikes, demoralized by the loss of the Krajina, and stretched across collapsing front lines, was in no condition to stop the Croatian Army: by 11 October the HVO Guards brigades had reached their stop line on the southern edge of Manjača, twenty-five kilometers from the city. Military commanders on the Federation side — particularly the ARBiH 5th Corps, which had endured three years of siege in Bihać and was now advancing with enormous momentum — resented the order to stop. Dudaković and Alagić would insist for years afterward that the West had robbed them of ground they could have taken, though it is doubtful the ARBiH could have gained much on its own against the reinforced VRS defenses around Prijedor and Banja Luka. From their perspective, the opportunity to recover territory seized through ethnic cleansing in 1992 was being sacrificed for diplomatic convenience.

Holbrooke's calculus was strategic rather than humanitarian in the conventional sense. A Federation capture of Banja Luka would have eliminated the territorial basis for a Bosnian Serb entity, making any negotiated settlement impossible. Serbian President Slobodan Milošević, who had been quietly acquiescing in the Federation advance as long as it compressed Republika Srpska toward a manageable size, would have been compelled to intervene — potentially reigniting a wider Balkan war. The 51-49 line, once achieved through military operations, needed to be frozen through diplomacy before the momentum of the offensive carried beyond the point of political utility.

The halt also reflected a broader American judgment about the nature of the peace that would follow. A settlement imposed by total military victory of one side would lack the buy-in necessary for implementation. Both entities needed to emerge from the war with enough territory and institutional structure to function, however imperfectly, within the framework of a single Bosnian state. The 51-49 split was not merely a cartographic convenience — it was judged to be the minimum territorial allocation that each side could accept without resuming the fight.

The ceasefire took effect on the morning of 12 October, but the lines did not freeze on the date Washington had set: in the west the fighting rumbled on for another week, Dudaković pressing his attack around Sanski Most until it faded to a fruitless finish on 20 October. Within weeks, the parties were at Wright-Patterson Air Force Base in Dayton, Ohio, negotiating under intense American pressure. The territorial map that emerged from those talks closely reflected the lines that existed when Holbrooke's phone call stopped the advance. The Dayton Agreement, signed in Paris on 14 December 1995, codified what the battlefield and diplomacy had jointly produced — a Bosnia divided along lines drawn not by any single peace plan, but by the calculated intersection of military force and political will.
